name: Insulin dosage
seoTitle: Insulin dosage Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Insulin dosage: work out total daily insulin dose from the carbohydrate content and the carbohydrate ratio. A free health calculator with the formula,…
summary: The Insulin dosage calculator turns the carbohydrate content, the carbohydrate ratio and the current blood glucose into total daily insulin dose. It suits an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. Change one value and the results step aside until you press Calculate again, which is what makes it easy to see how much the answer really depends on that one input.

sections.title: How does the Insulin dosage calculator work?
sections.html:
The Insulin dosage calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports total daily insulin dose in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the carbohydrate content (Step 1 - Carbohydrate coverage), the carbohydrate content (Step 1 - Carbohydrate coverage), the carbohydrate ratio (Step 1 - Carbohydrate coverage) and the current blood glucose (Step 2 - High blood sugar correction).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Insulin dosage calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Insulin dose to cover carbohydrates=carbohydrate content ÷ carbohydrate ratio
Insulin sensitivity factor=(current blood glucose − target blood glucose) ÷ insulin dose to correct blood glucose
Total insuline dose=insulin dose to correct blood glucose + insulin dose to cover carbohydrates
Carbohydrate ratio=carbohydrate content ÷ insulin dose to cover carbohydrates
Target blood glucose=-insulin dose to correct blood glucose × insulin sensitivity factor + current blood glucose
Carbohydrate ratio=500 ÷ total daily insulin dose

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Carbohydrate content = 10 g, Carbohydrate ratio = 10 g, Target blood glucose = 5.5556 Mg/d l and Insulin sensitivity factor = 2.8 Mg/d l. Working through the relationship above gives Insulin dose to cover carbohydrates = 1.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Insulin dose to cover carbohydrates = 1 should be roughly the size you expected from Carbohydrate content = 10 g and Carbohydrate ratio = 10 g.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Insulin dosage calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the carbohydrate content, the carbohydrate ratio and the current blood glucose — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Insulin dosage calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns total daily insulin dose, derived from the carbohydrate content, the carbohydrate ratio and the current blood glucose. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Insulin dosage calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the carbohydrate content, the carbohydrate ratio and the current blood glucose, which is 10 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter carbohydrate content (Step 1 - Carbohydrate coverage) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Carbohydrate content (Step 1 - Carbohydrate coverage) opens in grams and the chip beside it offers 29 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Insulin dose to cover carbohydrates = 1. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Insulin dosage calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
